Here is a summary of the live AMA session on wok cooking hosted by chef J. Kenji López-Alt:

---

### 1. Wok Physics & Materials vs. Western Pans

* *Heat Distribution:* Western pans and burners aim for flat, even, edge-to-edge heat across multi-ply clad metals (steel/aluminum/titanium). Wok burners use focused jets/vortices to concentrate heat at the bottom, creating distinct heat zones that decrease toward the cooler sides and form a rising hot-air column for moisture evaporation during tossing.
* *Why Carbon Steel is Best:* Carbon steel is a poor heat conductor (enabling concentrated heat at the bottom), lightweight, and durable under high-heat tossing and utensil impact compared to brittle cast iron.
* *Super Nitriding:* A process treating carbon steel with high heat and pressure in a nitrogen-rich environment, doubling its surface hardness, making it rust-resistant, non-reactive to acids, and smoother out of the box.

---

### 2. Wok Seasoning & Maintenance Myths

* *Seasoning Concept:* Unlike cast iron, which relies on building thick polymer layers over time, wok seasoning primarily focuses on converting raw carbon steel into a protective *black oxide* layer. High wok heat, metal expansion/warping, and acidic stir-fry sauces routinely strip soft polymer buildup.
* *Initial Seasoning:* Scrub away shipping oils from raw carbon steel, then heat until the surface turns blue-black (using gas, an oven at $450^\circ\text{F}+$, or a blowtorch).
* *Cleaning & Storage:* Wash with a scrub/bamboo brush (soap is fine; avoid harsh abrasives like Bar Keepers Friend). Reheat on the burner until fully dry, then rub in a paper-thin layer of neutral oil to prevent rust from ambient moisture.

---

### 3. Heat Sources, *Wok Hei*, & Induction

* *Understanding *Wok Hei (Breath of the Wok):** Flavor comes from food interacting with hot carbon steel, seared sauces along the edges, and aerosolized oil droplet ignition in an open flame.
* *Cooking on Induction / Electric:* While you can cook most dishes on induction, it lacks live flames for full *Wok Hei*. To cook effectively on induction, use your spatula to lift/tumble food instead of tossing off the cooktop, and consider finishing with a blowtorch over a sheet tray for a smoky touch.
* *Burner Focus:* Portable butane stoves ($12,500+\text{ BTU}$) often perform better indoors than standard flat Western burners because their flame ring is concentrated directly under the wok base.

---

### 4. Stir-Frying Technique & Batch Cooking

* *Tossing Motion:* Tossing follows four sub-movements: tilt near you, push forward horizontally, flick upward at the end, and pull back to cascade food through the hot air column. Practice using raw rice or beans.
* *Batching on Home Ranges:* Cook meat and vegetables in small batches ($\le \frac{1}{2}\text{ lb}$ / 8 oz) to keep the wok hot, transferring cooked components into a "landing bowl" or mesh strainer.
* *Texture over Browning:* Stir-frying prioritizes tender meat and crisp vegetables by driving off surface water without browning (flavor comes from fermented sauces like soy or oyster sauce). Re-combine all ingredients at the very end, adding sauces along the hot rim and using a starch slurry to emulsify grease into a smooth sauce.
